title: Build a Prompt Learning Loop - SallyAnn DeLucia & Fuad Ali, Arize

summary: SallyAnn DeLucia (Director of RISE at Arize) and Fuad Ali (Product Manager at Arize) lead a workshop on prompt learning, a method for continuously optimizing AI system prompts using rich textual feedback from evals and human annotations. They begin by explaining why agents fail—weak instructions, missing tools, poor planning, and context engineering gaps—and distinguish prompt learning from reinforcement learning and meta-prompting by its use of detailed textual feedback targeting specific prompt instructions. A coding agent case study demonstrates that adding structured engineering rules to Aider's system prompt improved performance by 15% without fine-tuning or architecture changes, with Claude 4.1 achieving near-4.5 performance at two-thirds the cost. They benchmark prompt learning against GABOR, finding it performs better in fewer loops, and emphasize that eval quality is foundational—agent and eval optimization loops should co-evolve. Audience Q&A covers eval design for non-coding tasks, multi-agent optimization, and overfitting reframed as desirable specialization. The workshop transitions to hands-on coding using a JSON webpage prompt example from the Arize RISE AI repo with OpenAI. Configuration includes sample size (default 100), 80/20 train-test split, number of rules, and optimization loops. The dataset contains input/output pairs with feedback fields. The speakers clarify that inputs can include conversation turns or tool-call context relevant to the step being optimized, but data from other pipeline steps should be excluded. They set up an initial basic system prompt and initialize two LLM-as-a-judge evaluators: a comprehensive output evaluator providing binary correct/incorrect labels with detailed explanations, and a granular rule checker examining per-rule compliance. Output generation uses OpenAI with JSON response format and temperature zero for consistency. The optimization loop is a three-part process: generate and evaluate outputs on test data, train and optimize using training-set feedback to improve the prompt, and iterate until a threshold or loop limit is met, tracking metrics across iterations. In the final section, the speakers walk through executing the optimization loop, which uses the prompt learning SDK optimizer to take in feedback, the original prompt, and produce an improved prompt. Results are saved to CSV and JSON files with iteration number, rule count, test/train accuracy scores, and all evaluation data. The last code block extracts the prompt achieving best test accuracy, showing the original and optimized versions side by side. The speakers note the workshop run takes 20-30 minutes with default settings but can be shortened to one loop (~6 minutes) for the workshop. They also highlight Arize's enterprise prompt optimization solution, where prompts live in a prompt hub, datasets with human annotations or evals are attached, and the system produces optimized prompt versions automatically—useful for teams not wanting to maintain custom code loops.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Introductions and Agenda
sections.summary: SallyAnn DeLucia (Director of RISE) and Fuad Ali (Product Manager) introduce themselves, their technical backgrounds, and the workshop agenda covering agent failures, prompt learning, a case study, GRPO comparison, and hands-on coding.

sections.title: Why Agents Fail Today
sections.summary: Audience polling shows most build agents but few find them reliable. Core failure causes include weak instructions, missing tools, poor planning, and context engineering gaps. An organizational split between technical users and domain experts must be bridged by prompt learning.

sections.title: What Is Prompt Learning
sections.summary: Prompt learning is contrasted with reinforcement learning (scalar reward, weight updates) and meta-prompting (score-based prompt updates). Prompt learning feeds the LLM rich textual feedback—human annotations and LLM-as-a-judge reasoning—to target specific system prompt instructions.

sections.title: Coding Agent Case Study
sections.summary: A case study on coding agents shows Aider with Claude 3.5 at ~30% vs ~40% for SOTA. Adding structured engineering rules to the system prompt improved correctness.

sections.title: Case Study Results and Overfitting Discussion
sections.summary: Benchmarking showed 15% improvement from rules alone. Claude 4.1 achieved near-4.5 performance at two-thirds cost. Overfitting is reframed as building expertise with train-test splits ensuring generalization.

sections.title: GABOR Benchmarking and Eval Quality
sections.summary: GABOR is benchmarked against prompt learning, which performs better in fewer loops. Eval quality is emphasized as foundational—optimizing eval prompts is as important as optimizing agent prompts.

sections.title: Audience Q&A on Eval Design and Rule Refinement
sections.summary: Audience questions address eval design for non-coding tasks, continuous rule refinement, and simulator vs end-to-end evaluation. Prompt learning is an ongoing cycle of failure collection, annotation, and prompt optimization.

sections.title: Co-Evolving Loops and Evals-Not-Blocking Philosophy
sections.summary: Two co-evolving loops are introduced: blue for agent optimization and orange for eval optimization. Evals should never block getting started—build scrappy prototypes first, then refine iteratively.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Prompt Learning and Overfitting as Specialization
sections.summary: Current prompt learning optimizes independent tasks in isolation, with future multi-agent coordination. Overfitting on a code base is reframed as desirable specialization.

sections.title: Hands-On Coding Workshop Setup
sections.summary: The speakers transition to hands-on coding using a JSON webpage prompt example from the Arize RISE AI repo. Attendees clone the repo, set up OpenAI API keys, install dependencies, and add async execution.

sections.title: Configuration and Dataset Walkthrough
sections.summary: Configuration parameters are explained: sample size, train-test split, number of rules, and optimization loops. The dataset includes input/output pairs with feedback fields using an 80/20 split. A participant asks whether inputs can be chat histories.

sections.title: Input Data Scope and Context Inclusion Discussion
sections.summary: The speakers clarify that inputs should be one-to-one for simple cases, but conversation-level inputs are possible. For multi-turn conversations, each turn can be an independent row. Context and tool-call data flowing into the prompt step being optimized should be included, but data from other pipeline steps should be excluded.

sections.title: Initial System Prompt and Evaluator Setup
sections.summary: An initial basic system prompt for JSON webpage creation is set up. Two LLM-as-a-judge evaluators are initialized: a comprehensive output evaluator providing binary correct/incorrect labels with detailed explanations, and a granular rule checker examining per-rule compliance. Both generate feedback for the optimization loop.

sections.title: Evaluator Code Walkthrough
sections.summary: The evaluator code is shown, including reading rules from a file, using OpenAI as the LLM provider, classification evaluator setup with correct/incorrect choices, optional score mapping, and a template. Participants are reminded to use their own OpenAI keys.

sections.title: Output Generation Function
sections.summary: The output generation function is explained: it uses OpenAI with JSON response format and temperature zero for consistent outputs, takes a dataset and system prompt, generates outputs for all rows, and returns results for evaluation during each iteration.

sections.title: Additional Metrics and Optimization Loop Introduction
sections.summary: Optional classification metrics (accuracy, F1, precision, recall) are calculated from binary score mappings. The optimization loop is introduced as a three-part process: generate and evaluate on test data, train and optimize using training-set feedback to improve the prompt, and iterate until a threshold or loop limit is met, tracking metrics across iterations.

sections.title: Optimization Loop Execution and Result Saving
sections.summary: The optimization loop is executed using the prompt learning SDK optimizer, which takes in feedback (correctness, explanation, rule violations), the original prompt, and context size limits to produce an improved prompt. The loop generates outputs, evaluates them, and repeats until threshold or max loops. Results are saved to CSV and JSON with iteration number, rule count, test/train accuracy scores, and all evaluation data. The full run takes approximately 20-30 minutes; reducing loops to one takes about 6 minutes.

sections.title: Best Prompt Extraction and Enterprise Solution
sections.summary: The final code block extracts the prompt achieving best test accuracy, showing original and optimized versions for deployment. The speakers highlight Arize's enterprise prompt optimization solution with a prompt hub, datasets with human annotations or evals, and automated optimized prompt versioning for teams that prefer not to maintain custom code loops. Workshop troubleshooting guidance includes pinning package version to 2.2 and using nestio for faster execution.

limitations: Reinforcement learning is difficult to apply to prompt optimization because updating LLM weights directly is impractical
Meta-prompting alone is insufficient because it only uses scores, not rich textual feedback
GABOR, while using positive reflection, still underperforms prompt learning and requires more loops
Unreliable evals undermine the entire prompt optimization pipeline—eval prompt quality is a critical dependency
Static instructions do not scale for sustainable agent performance
Current prompt learning operates on independent tasks in isolation; multi-agent coordination not yet supported
Off-the-shelf evals are a starting point but require iterative refinement to be reliable
Including irrelevant conversation data or context from other pipeline steps can reduce optimization effectiveness
Maintaining custom code loops and task infrastructure can be difficult for teams without dedicated engineering resources
Package version issues can cause errors during workshop setup, requiring specific version pinning
